title: Who’s next to go? We answer your questions on MLB’s managerial madness
content:
I just spent the past few days in Toronto watching a team that had just fired its once-popular manager, and while I was there, another team fired its once-popular manager. All before May 1.

So, Alex Cora is no longer managing the Red Sox, Rob Thomson is no longer managing the Phillies, and with Andy McCullough on paternity leave, I’m now here answering questions about who else might be on the managerial hot seat. Here we go. Some questions have been edited in the name of clarity (and occasionally in the name of brevity).

I wonder if any particular name will be mentioned more than once.

Sure, Mets manager Carlos Mendoza is one skipper on the hot seat. He was sitting pretty in 2024 when the Mets made the NLCS in his first season, but the Mets missed the playoffs last year, and they had the same record as the Phillies on the day Thomson was fired. So, that’s not great. Plus, Mendoza is in the final guaranteed year of his contract, making it even easier for the Mets to cut ties and move on. But a lot of teams are underperforming, so let’s check in with some other readers.

Does a Hall of Famer really want to step into this mess?

I mean, come on, that’s not even how this works.

Wait, is David Wright a possibility? I asked Mets beat writer Tim Britton.

“Wright dabbled in being a special assistant shortly after he retired,” Tim said, “but ever since, he’s been very content spending time with his family in California. He hasn’t even wanted the special assistant grind, let alone the manager one.”

So much for that. Moving on.

There actually does seem to be a consensus forming.

We posted our “Who do you think will be next?” question on Sunday, less than 24 hours after Cora was axed, and most responses focused on two names: Thomson and Mendoza. Before we could respond, Thomson was out, leaving Mendoza as the most obvious managerial firing candidate in the game.

To be up front, I really like Mendoza. I covered him almost two decades ago when he was a minor league utility man and I was a Triple A beat writer, and even then, as a minor league journeyman bench player, Mendoza was enormously respected. Of the hundreds of players I covered in the minor leagues, I can think of two who stood out as future managers: Mendoza and A.J. Hinch. (Actually, Dusty Wathan struck me as that type of guy, too, and now he’s the Phillies’ bench coach; and in retrospect, I can see it with Shelley Duncan who’s now managing in Triple A and has an intense love for the sport.)

Point is, I take no pleasure in considering Mendoza’s uncertain job status. He’s smart and engaging and easy to like.

But the Red Sox twice hired Cora to be their manager, and I really believe ownership still thinks he’s one of the best in the business. Thomson is as likable as a University of Kansas guy could possibly be — MIZ! — and he took the Phillies to the playoffs four years in a row. But managerial jobs aren’t popularity contests, especially not in markets like Boston, Philadelphia and New York.

First, is there any chance this question is from 2007 Yankees spot starter Chase Wright? No, right? It’s weird that I even thought about it? OK.

David Stearns was among the sport’s most in-demand baseball executives when the Mets hired him away from the Brewers in 2023. Pairing his small-market know-how with Steve Cohen’s Big Apple money felt like the most significant front office move since Andrew Friedman left the Rays for the Dodgers and quickly built a behemoth.

But Stearns hasn’t had that kind of success, at least not right out of the gate. He and Mendoza started together with that stunning playoff run in 2024, but last season was a disappointment (after the Mets shelled out for Juan Soto) and this year has been even worse (after a radical transformation that included signing Bo Bichette, trading Brandon Nimmo and Jeff McNeil, and letting Pete Alonso and Edwin Díaz walk in free agency). Both Alonso and Díaz have underperformed, but that’s not the Mets’ concern. Their lineup is a mess, their rotation is top-heavy, and their record is worse than the Rockies, White Sox and Nationals.

So, why does Stearns still have a job? Well, it’s not like this is the first Mets team to spend a lot of Cohen’s money without much to show for it, and Stearns was a big enough get that his leash is surely longer than one bad season plus one atrocious month.

Beyond Thomson and Mendoza, these were the only other names singled out by our readers: Matt Quatraro of the Royals and Joe Espada of the Astros. Quatraro was Manager of the Year runner-up in 2024, and Espada got down-ballot Manager of the Year votes each of the past two years. Just a reminder of how fickle these jobs can be.

By the way, have I mentioned that I don’t know anyone who particularly enjoys voting for Manager of the Year? It’s just so difficult to judge. Each job carries its own quirks and challenges. But anyway…

It’s worth noting that FanGraphs — to name one objective source of analysis — wasn’t particularly sold on either the Royals or the Astros this season. Preseason projections had both hovering right around .500 (Royals a game or so over, the Astros a game or so under). Each has been far worse than that and playing at roughly the same pace as the Red Sox.

Three-fifths of Kansas City’s rotation has been pretty good, but Cole Ragans is off to a bad start, and Vinnie Pasquantino is not hitting much at all. For the Astros, Yordan Alvarez is an early MVP candidate but the outfield is a predictable problem and the pitching staff is a complete wreck of injuries and underperformance (and both in the case of Tatsuya Imai).

From the outside, of those two, I’d say that Espada feels like the one most on the hot seat, but I’m also not sure that the Astros problems are going to be solved by having a new voice in the clubhouse, and Astros GM Dana Brown defended Espada this weekend. So, he seems safe, at least for now.

Within an hour of the Cora firing on Saturday, I got a text message from a baseball guy: “He might be the Phils skipper by Monday.” Of course, that’s not the way it played out. Cora turned down the Phillies gig and has told any reporter who will listen that he’s quite happy to go home and watch his kids play ball for the summer. According to our own reporting: Cora feared the Phillies would not get the best version of himself.

But how long will that last? It might last through the season at least. Cora’s getting paid, he’s already won a World Series as a player, coach and manager, and his twin boys turn 9 this summer (as the father of a 9-year-old myself, I can say the prospect of a few low-stakes months watching him play ball would be difficult to turn down).

The Phillies gig was a pretty natural fit for Cora given his relationship with Dave Dombrowski and the potential to win right away if things turn around. If Cora couldn’t be coaxed to Philadelphia, I doubt he’ll be convinced to manage anywhere else this year. But, come the offseason, he’ll be one of the most in-demand free agents on the market.

That’s a really interesting question. One person close to the Red Sox situation texted in the aftermath of the firing to say that he thought outfield instructor and third-base coach Kyle Hudson might be the interim manager, then he saw that Hudson was one of the guys fired. Also fired/reassigned/clearly not in the mix: Jason Varitek, the iconic Red Sox catcher who many expected to manage the team at some point.

So, who else?

Of course, there’s some chance the team thrives under interim manager Chad Tracy — who cut his teeth managing for the Red Sox in Triple A — and that Tracy earned the trust of chief baseball officer Craig Breslow (players already love the guy). But let’s assume the Red Sox want a bigger name with more experience. David Ross and Rocco Baldelli stand out as former managers who have had big league success and carry Red Sox ties. There’s also George Lombard, the highly regarded Tigers bench coach who worked as a manager and coordinator in the Red Sox minor league system (let’s see, do the Red Sox have any history of hiring A.J. Hinch’s bench coach?).

Really, it comes down to Breslow, assuming this Red Sox season doesn’t cost him his job as well. This feels like a situation in which a hard-to-predict, off-the-board choice could be incoming.

Presumably, this question is about managers going from one Major League team to another — like, if Cora had been fired by the Red Sox and become manager of the Phillies — in which case, the most famous example is probably Bob Lemon, the Hall of Fame lefty who began his career as a position player before moving to the mound and collecting 207 wins in basically 12 years.

Lemon last pitched in 1958 and became a manager in 1970. In 1978, he was fired by the White Sox. The Yankees hired him less than a month later. Those were the Yankees of Reggie Jackson, Graig Nettles and Thurmon Munson; of Ron Guidry, Goose Gossage and Catfish Hunter. Billy Martin had been their manager at the start of the season, and they would go on to win the ’78 World Series under Lemon.

So, has a manager ever switched teams mid-season and how did it work out? Yes, it’s happened, and it’s worked out pretty well. But as you said, this is more of a Stark question, so let’s ask him. Any other examples we should know about, Jayson?

“The other is Buck Rodgers, with the Expos and Angels,” Stark says, “The GM who fired him in Montreal was … Dave D!”

Weird and wild, indeed. And I think we’ve got time for one more question and/or comment. Take it away:

Alright. You know what? That’s my fault. This seems to have run its course. See you next week.
